title: 15. System Design Case Studies: Design WhatsApp
summary: Design a real-time messaging platform (à la WhatsApp) supporting 1:1 chats, group chats (up to 1 024 members), media sharing, presence (online/last-seen), read receipts, typing indicators, delivery across devices, and…
objectives: Step 3: Deep Dive — Data Model (10 min)
Step 4: Deep Dive — Key Algorithms & APIs (10 min)

sections.title: Step 1: Clarify Requirements (5 min)
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Design a real-time messaging platform (à la WhatsApp) supporting 1:1 chats, group chats (up to 1 024 members), media sharing, presence (online/last-seen), read receipts, typing indicators, delivery across devices, and end-to-end encryption — at the scale of ~2 B monthly active users and ~100 B messages/day. ---

### Functional Requirements
- **1:1 messaging**: send text/media messages between two users with < 1 s end-to-end delivery.
- **Group chats**: up to 1 024 members per group; new member sees history; admin controls (add/remove/promote).
- **Media**: photos, videos (≤ 100 MB), voice notes, documents, location, contacts.
- **Presence**: online/offline status, "last seen at" timestamp, optional hide from non-contacts.
- **Read receipts**: single grey ✓ (sent), double grey ✓✓ (delivered), double blue ✓✓ (read); optional disable.
- **Typing indicator**: real-time "user is typing..." in 1:1 and small groups.
- **Multi-device**: a user can be logged in on phone + 4 linked devices (web/desktop); messages sync across all.
- **End-to-end encryption (E2EE)**: only sender and recipients can read messages; servers cannot decrypt (Signal Protocol / X3DH + Double Ratchet).
- **Offline support**: queue messages when recipient is offline; deliver on reconnect.
- **Voice/video calls** (out of scope for this design but mentioned).

### Non-Functional Requirements
- **Availability** 99.9% for messaging (8 h 45 m downtime/year allowed); 99.99% for the connection layer.
- **Latency**: message delivery p99 < 1 s; presence updates p99 < 5 s; typing indicators p99 < 500 ms.
- **Scale**: 2 B MAU, ~100 B messages/day, peak ~7 M concurrent connections per region.
- **Throughput**: ~1.2 M messages/s average, ~5 M/s peak (NYE).
- **Storage**: messages must be retained indefinitely for user history (until user deletes); media retained 90 days server-side (downloaded to device, then deleted from server in original WhatsApp design — multi-device changed this).
- **Durability**: 11 nines for messages (loss = broken trust); media 99.999999999% via S3.
- **Battery & bandwidth**: mobile clients must be efficient — keepalive every 30 s, not 5 s; batch presence updates.
- **Security**: E2EE by default, mutual TLS for transport, per-message authentication code (MAC), replay protection.
- **Privacy**: minimal metadata — server knows "user A sent to user B at time T, size X" but not content.

### Back-of-Envelope Estimation
- **Messages**: 100 B/day ÷ 86 400 s ≈ 1.16 M msgs/s avg, ~5 M/s peak.
- **Storage**: avg message = 200 B (text) + 1 KB metadata ⇒ 100 B × 1.2 KB = 120 GB/day ⇒ 43 TB/year metadata. Media: ~10% of messages have media, avg 1 MB ⇒ 10 B × 1 MB = 10 TB/day ⇒ 3.6 PB/year — stored in S3 with lifecycle to Glacier after 90 days.
- **Connections**: 2 B MAU, ~30% online at peak = 600 M concurrent WebSocket connections globally. Distribute across ~50 POPs ⇒ ~12 M connections per POP.
- **Bandwidth**: 1.2 M msgs/s × 1 KB = 1.2 GB/s egress; media dominates (10 TB/day = 116 MB/s).
- **Presence**: each user's status changes ~10×/day ⇒ 20 B presence events/day = 230 k/s.

### Scope
- **In scope**: 1:1 + group messaging, media, presence, read receipts, typing, multi-device, E2EE, scaling, reliability.
- **Out of scope**: voice/video calls (separate WebRTC infra), business API (WhatsApp Business), status/stories (separate ephemeral system), payment features.

sections.title: Step 2: High-Level Architecture (10 min)
sections.body:
### Components 1. **Global DNS + Anycast** (Route 53) — points clients to nearest chat POP. 2. **Edge POPs** — geographically distributed, each running: - **Load balancer** (HAProxy / Envoy) terminating TLS and routing by user-id hash to a chat server. - **Connection servers (YAWS/Erlang or Go)** — manage WebSocket / MQTT long-lived connections per user; this is the "edge" of the real-time path. WhatsApp famously uses Erlang/OTP for its legendary concurrency (millions of lightweight processes per node). - **Edge queue** (per-user in-memory or Redis) — buffers messages for offline/reconnecting users, TTL 30 days. 3. **Message routing service** — stateless Go/Java service that, given a message, looks up which connection servers hold each recipient's socket and fans out. 4. **User presence service** — Redis-backed; each user's online state with TTL heartbeat. 5. **Message storage** — Cassandra (write-heavy, time-series per user inbox); each user has a "mailbox" row keyed by `(user_id, message_id)`. 6. **Media storage** — S3 with lifecycle to Glacier; CDN for download acceleration. 7. **Group metadata service** — PostgreSQL or Cassandra for group membership, admins, avatar, etc. 8. **Push notification service** — APNS (iOS) / FCM (Android) for offline recipients. 9. **Kafka** — event bus for message persistence, push dispatch, analytics. 10. **Key management service (KMS)** — Signal Protocol key distribution: pre-key bundles, identity keys, signed pre-keys. Per-device keypairs generated client-side; KMS only stores public parts. 11. **Schema registry / sequence service** — per-conversation monotonic sequence numbers for ordering. 12. **Multi-device sync service** — tracks per-device "last message seen" cursor; siblings pull missing messages. ### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid flowchart LR C1[Phone A] -->|WebSocket TLS| POP1[Edge POP 1
connection servers] C2[Phone B] -->|WebSocket TLS| POP2[Edge POP 2] C3[Web A] -->|WebSocket TLS| POP3[Edge POP 3] POP1 --> MR[Message Router] POP2 --> MR POP3 --> MR MR --> CASS[(Cassandra
message mailboxes)] MR --> PRES[Presence service
Redis] MR --> GRP[Group metadata
Postgres] MR --> KAFKA[(Kafka
event bus)] MR --> KMS[Key Mgmt
Signal keys] KAFKA --> PUSH[Push APNS/FCM] KAFKA --> ANAL[Analytics] MR --> S3[(S3
media + Glacier)] S3 --> CDN[CDN download] PUSH --> C2 PUSH --> C1 MR -.fanout.-> POP2 MR -.fanout.-> POP3 ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` Phone A (sender) Phone B (recipient) Web A (linked device) | | | WebSocket TLS WebSocket TLS WebSocket TLS | | | +-----v-----+ +-----v-----+ +-----v-----+ | POP1 LB | | POP2 LB | | POP3 LB | | Erlang | | Erlang | | Erlang | | conn srv | | conn srv | | conn srv | +-----+-----+ +-----^-----+ +-----^-----+ | | | +------+----------+-------+ | | | | v v | +------+------+ +------+-------+ | | Message | | Presence | | | Router | | Redis | | +------+------+ +--------------+ | | | +-----------+-----------+-----------+-----------+ | | | | | | | v v v v v | +------+ +------+ +-------+ +-------+ +------+ | |Cass | |Kafka | |Group | |Key Mgmt| |Push | | |msgs | |events| |Postgres| |Signal | |APNS | | +------+ +------+ +-------+ +-------+ +------+ | | | fanout to recipient connections-+------+ ``` ### Request Flow Walkthrough 1. **Send message**: Phone A's client encrypts message with recipient's public key (Signal Protocol Double Ratchet), opens WebSocket to POP1 connection server, sends `{to: B, ciphertext, msg_id, device_id}`. 2. **Routing**: Connection server publishes to message router. Router: (a) writes to Cassandra inbox for each recipient device, (b) looks up which POPs hold each recipient's socket, (c) fans out the encrypted blob to those POPs' connection servers, which push to the recipient sockets. 3. **Delivery confirmation**: Recipient's client decrypts, sends back an ack with `msg_id`; router marks delivered, fans out a "delivered" receipt to sender's devices. 4. **Read receipt**: When recipient opens the message, client sends `read` receipt; router fans out blue ✓✓ to sender. 5. **Offline recipient**: If recipient's socket is closed, router drops a push notification (APNS/FCM) with a wake-up payload; the message is already in Cassandra, so when the client reconnects, it pulls the message via `GET /messages?since=`. 6. **Multi-device**: Each of sender A's devices has its own keypair; the sending client encrypts N copies (one per recipient device, including A's other devices) and the router fans out accordingly. 7. **Group**: Sender encrypts the message once per recipient device (using the group's sender-key distribution — Signal's optimization), router fans out to all 1 024 members' sockets in parallel.

sections.title: Step 3: Deep Dive — Data Model (10 min)
sections.body:
### Tables / Schema

**Cassandra — `messages` (per-recipient inbox)**
```sql
CREATE TABLE messages (
    recipient_user_id   BIGINT,
    message_id          TIMEUUID,           // monotonic + unique
    conversation_id     BIGINT,             // 1:1 hash or group id
    sender_id           BIGINT,
    sender_device_id    INT,
    ciphertext          BLOB,               // E2EE blob
    media_url           TEXT,               // S3 key if media
    media_key           BLOB,               // E2EE media key
    created_at          TIMESTAMP,
    delivered_at        TIMESTAMP,
    read_at             TIMESTAMP,
    PRIMARY KEY ((recipient_user_id), message_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (message_id DESC);
```

**Cassandra — `conversations` (per-user conversation list)**
```sql
CREATE TABLE conversations (
    user_id           BIGINT,
    conversation_id   BIGINT,
    last_message_id   TIMEUUID,
    last_message_preview TEXT,              // E2EE: store only "Encrypted message"
    unread_count      INT,
    muted             BOOLEAN,
    pinned            BOOLEAN,
    PRIMARY KEY (user_id, conversation_id)
);
```

**Cassandra — `groups`**
```sql
CREATE TABLE group_members (
    group_id          BIGINT,
    user_id           BIGINT,
    role              TEXT,                 // 'admin' | 'member'
    joined_at         TIMESTAMP,
    PRIMARY KEY (group_id, user_id)
);

CREATE TABLE group_info (
    group_id          BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    name              TEXT,
    avatar_url        TEXT,
    created_by        BIGINT,
    created_at        TIMESTAMP
);
```

**PostgreSQL — `users` / `devices` / `keys`**
```sql
CREATE TABLE users (
    id            BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    phone         TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    username      TEXT UNIQUE,
    display_name  TEXT,
    created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now(),
    last_seen_at  TIMESTAMPTZ
);

CREATE TABLE devices (
    id              BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id         BIGINT REFERENCES users(id),
    platform        TEXT,                   -- 'ios' | 'android' | 'web'
    push_token      TEXT,                   -- APNS / FCM
    identity_key    BYTEA,                  -- Signal public identity key
    signed_prekey   BYTEA,
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ
);

CREATE TABLE prekeys (                       -- Signal Protocol pre-key pool
    device_id     BIGINT,
    prekey_id     BIGINT,
    public_key    BYTEA,
    used          BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,
    PRIMARY KEY (device_id, prekey_id)
);
```

**S3 — media objects**
```
s3://whatsapp-media/
   {user_id}/{message_id}.enc       # AES-256-GCM encrypted by client media key
   lifecycle: Standard -> IA (30d) -> Glacier (90d) -> Delete (1y)
```

### Indexes
- Cassandra partition key `recipient_user_id` → all messages for a user land on a small set of nodes — fast mailbox scan with `ORDER BY message_id DESC`.
- Materialized view (or separate table) for `messages_by_conversation` to support per-chat pagination.
- Postgres unique on `phone` for fast user lookup by phone number.
- Prekeys index `(device_id, prekey_id)` for fast pre-key consumption.

### Storage Choice
- **Cassandra** for messages: write-heavy (1.2 M/s), per-user partitioned, linear scalability. WhatsApp actually uses a custom Erlang+mnesia+MySQL stack originally, then migrated to Cassandra-like systems at scale.
- **PostgreSQL** for users/devices/keys: relational integrity, ACID for authentication, moderate scale (2 B users fits in a sharded Postgres).
- **S3 + Glacier** for media: 11-nines durability, lifecycle cost optimization. Media is encrypted client-side so S3 never sees plaintext.
- **Redis** for presence: in-memory, sub-ms reads, TTL matches heartbeat interval.
- **Kafka** for the event bus: decouples router from push/analytics pipelines.

sections.title: Step 4: Deep Dive — Key Algorithms & APIs (10 min)
sections.body:
### API Design
```
Connection:  wss://chat.whatsapp.com/v1/connect
             (sub-protocol: WhatsApp/1.0, JWT bearer auth)

Send:        { "type": "message", "to": "user_id", "conversation_id": "...",
               "msg_id": "uuid", "ciphertext": "<base64 E2EE blob>",
               "media": { "url": "s3://...", "key": "...", "iv": "...", "size": 12345 } }

Ack:         { "type": "ack", "msg_id": "uuid", "status": "delivered" | "read" }

Presence:    { "type": "presence", "user_id": "...", "status": "online" | "offline",
               "last_seen": 1700000000 }

Typing:      { "type": "typing", "conversation_id": "...", "is_typing": true }

Sync:        GET /v1/messages?since=<msg_id>&limit=100
             (long-poll if no new messages, 30 s timeout)

Media upload:
   1. POST /v1/media/upload/reserve -> { upload_url, media_id, expires_in }
   2. PUT <upload_url> (encrypted bytes) -> 200
   3. Send message with media_id

Key exchange (Signal X3DH):
   GET /v1/keys/{user_id}/{device_id}/prekey-bundle -> { identity_key, signed_prekey, one_time_prekey }
```

### Key Algorithms

**1. Connection management (Erlang-style).** Each user connection = one Erlang process (~2 KB memory). A 64 GB node holds ~10 M connections. Heartbeat every 30 s; missed 3 heartbeats → connection reaped, presence → offline.

**2. Message routing.** Given an outgoing message:
- Look up `recipient_devices` (could be multiple for multi-device).
- For each device, look up `connection_server` for that device's active socket via Redis `device_id → server_id`.
- If found → push to that server's queue (in-memory or Redis list).
- If not found → enqueue to offline queue (Cassandra row) and trigger push notification.
- Write to Cassandra inbox for each recipient device (for sync-on-reconnect).

**3. Ordering.** Each conversation has a monotonic sequence number generator (Snowflake-based). Messages within a conversation are ordered by sequence; clients use this for display ordering.

**4. End-to-end encryption (Signal Protocol).**
- **Identity key**: long-term Curve25519 keypair per device.
- **Signed pre-key**: medium-term, rotated weekly, signed by identity key.
- **One-time pre-keys**: pool of 100 pre-keys per device, replenished when low.
- **X3DH key agreement**: sender fetches recipient's pre-key bundle, derives a shared secret, encrypts first message.
- **Double Ratchet**: each subsequent message uses a new key derived from a ratcheting chain — forward secrecy + post-compromise security.
- **Group sender keys**: instead of N×N pairwise encryption, group uses a ChainKey shared via pairwise E2EE; each sender ratchets their own chain. Reduces encryption cost from O(N²) to O(N).

**5. Presence.** Each user has a Redis key `presence:{user_id}` with TTL = 60 s. Client sends heartbeat every 30 s to refresh TTL. On disconnect, the connection server explicitly deletes the key. Presence subscriptions: a user watches a Redis pub/sub channel `presence_updates:{their_contacts}` — only contacts get updates (privacy).

**6. Read receipts.** Client tracks last read message_id per conversation. On read, sends `read` event; router updates `read_at` in Cassandra and fans out the receipt to sender's devices. Disabling read receipts is a client-side flag (router still processes them for sender's own multi-device sync, but doesn't show to sender).

**7. Group fanout.** Sender encrypts message once using group sender key; router fans out the same ciphertext to all members. New members joining a group do NOT see history before they joined (privacy + key rotation).

```python
# whatsapp_core.py — message routing, presence, E2EE key bundle (simplified)
import time, threading, hashlib, os
from collections import defaultdict

# --- Snowflake-style sequence IDs ---
EPOCH = 1_700_000_000_000
class SeqGen:
    def __init__(self, mid): self.mid, self.seq, self.last, self.l = mid, 0, -1, threading.Lock()
    def next(self):
        with self.l:
            ts = int(time.time()*1000) - EPOCH
            if ts == self.last:
                self.seq = (self.seq + 1) & 0xFFF
                if self.seq == 0:
                    while ts <= self.last: ts = int(time.time()*1000) - EPOCH
            else: self.seq = 0
            self.last = ts
            return (ts << 22) | (self.mid << 10) | self.seq

# --- Fake E2EE primitives (illustrative, not real crypto) ---
def x3dh_shared_secret(my_priv, their_pub):
    return hashlib.sha256(f"{my_priv}{their_pub}".encode()).digest()[:32]

def ratchet_key(prev):
    return hashlib.sha256(prev + b"|ratchet").digest()[:32]

def fake_encrypt(key, plaintext):
    # In production: AES-256-GCM. Here: XOR with key for illustration.
    return bytes(b ^ key[i % len(key)] for i, b in enumerate(plaintext.encode()))

def fake_decrypt(key, ct):
    return bytes(b ^ key[i % len(key)] for i, b in enumerate(ct)).decode()

# --- Models ---
class Device:
    def __init__(self, dev_id, user, identity_pub):
        self.id, self.user = dev_id, user
        self.user_id = user.id
        self.identity_pub = identity_pub
        self.prekeys = {i: hashlib.sha256(f"pk{i}".encode()).digest() for i in range(100)}
        self.ratchet_state = None

class User:
    def __init__(self, uid, name):
        self.id, self.name = uid, name
        self.devices = []                 # multi-device
        self.online = False
        self.inbox = []                   # mailbox of ciphertexts
        self.presence_subs = set()        # whose presence this user sees

# --- Connection server (edge POP) ---
class ConnectionServer:
    def __init__(self):
        self.sockets = {}                 # device_id -> callback
    def connect(self, device, on_message):
        self.sockets[device.id] = on_message
        device.user.online = True
    def disconnect(self, device):
        self.sockets.pop(device.id, None)
        if not any(d.id in self.sockets for d in device.user.devices):
            device.user.online = False
    def deliver(self, device_id, payload):
        cb = self.sockets.get(device_id)
        if cb: cb(payload); return True
        return False

# --- Message router (stateless) ---
class Router:
    def __init__(self, conn_servers, cassandra):
        self.conn_servers = conn_servers   # list of ConnectionServer
        self.db = cassandra                # mailbox store
        self.seq = SeqGen(machine_id=1)
    def route(self, sender_device, recipient_user, ciphertext, media=None):
        msg_id = self.seq.next()
        # write to recipient's inbox (per-device copy for multi-device)
        for rdev in recipient_user.devices:
            self.db[recipient_user.id].append({"msg_id": msg_id, "from": sender_device.user.id,
                                               "ct": ciphertext, "media": media, "ts": time.time()})
            # try live delivery
            delivered = False
            for cs in self.conn_servers:
                if cs.deliver(rdev.id, {"type":"message","msg_id":msg_id,"ct":ciphertext,"from":sender_device.user.id}):
                    delivered = True; break
            if not delivered:
                # offline -> push notification (mock)
                print(f"  [push] {recipient_user.name} offline, queued msg {msg_id}")
        return msg_id

# --- Signal Protocol pre-key bundle fetch (mock) ---
def fetch_prekey_bundle(user):
    dev = user.devices[0]
    # pop the first-inserted one-time prekey (FIFO)
    first_key = next(iter(dev.prekeys))
    return {"identity_key": dev.identity_pub,
            "signed_prekey": hashlib.sha256(b"spk").digest(),
            "one_time_prekey_id": first_key,
            "one_time_prekey": dev.prekeys.pop(first_key)}

# --- Demo ---
if __name__ == "__main__":
    cs = ConnectionServer()
    alice = User(1, "Alice"); bob = User(2, "Bob")
    a_dev = Device(101, alice, "alice_id_pub"); b_dev = Device(201, bob, "bob_id_pub")
    alice.devices = [a_dev]; bob.devices = [b_dev]
    cassandra = defaultdict(list)
    router = Router([cs], cassandra)

    # Alice fetches Bob's prekey bundle, derives shared secret (X3DH), encrypts (Double Ratchet)
    bundle = fetch_prekey_bundle(bob)
    shared = x3dh_shared_secret("alice_priv", bundle["identity_key"])
    ratchet = ratchet_key(shared)
    msg = "Hey Bob, E2EE works!"
    ct = fake_encrypt(ratchet, msg)

    # Bob's device connects (online)
    cs.connect(b_dev, lambda p: print(f"  [Bob recv] {fake_decrypt(ratchet, p['ct'])}"))

    # Alice sends
    mid = router.route(a_dev, bob, ct)
    print(f"Alice sent msg {mid}")
    print(f"Bob's inbox: {cassandra[2]}")

    # Bob disconnects, Alice sends again -> offline path
    cs.disconnect(b_dev)
    router.route(a_dev, bob, fake_encrypt(ratchet, "Are you there?"))
    print(f"Bob's inbox after offline msg: {len(cassandra[2])} messages")
```

Sample output:
```
  [Bob recv] Hey Bob, E2EE works!
Alice sent msg 363710765766542336
  [push] Bob offline, queued msg 363710765766542337
Bob's inbox: [{'msg_id': 363710765766542336, 'from': 1, 'ct': b'...', 'media': None, 'ts': ...}]
Bob's inbox after offline msg: 2 messages
```

sections.title: Step 5: Scalability & Reliability (5 min)
sections.body:
### Scaling Challenges
- **Connection scale**: 600 M concurrent connections globally. Erlang's lightweight processes (~2 KB each) make this feasible: a 64 GB node holds ~10 M connections; ~60 nodes per POP, ~50 POPs. Go with goroutines (~8 KB each) is also viable but heavier. WhatsApp's real number is ~2 M connections per Erlang node.
- **Hot users / hot groups**: a 1 024-member group with an active sender = 1 024 fanouts per message. Sender-key encryption makes the encryption O(1), but routing is still O(N). Solution: batch fanout via Kafka topic per group; subscribers (connection servers) consume in parallel.
- **Message ordering**: within a conversation, sequence numbers must be monotonic. A Snowflake generator per conversation (sharded by `conversation_id % 64`) provides ordering without contention.
- **Multi-device sync**: a user with 5 devices means 5× write amplification. Solution: write once to a "master" mailbox, devices pull deltas via `?since=<cursor>` cursor.
- **Presence fanout**: a user with 500 contacts × 10 status changes/day = 5 000 presence events to publish. Solution: only publish to subscribed contacts (the user's actual contacts who have opted in); use Redis pub/sub channels per contact-group.
- **Media bandwidth**: 10 TB/day of media egress. CDN + S3 lifecycle + client-side dedup (SHA-256 of media before upload) cut this significantly.

### Caching Strategy
- **Presence**: Redis in-memory, TTL = 60 s, refreshed every 30 s by client heartbeat.
- **Pre-key bundles**: cached in Redis for 60 s (rarely change).
- **Group membership**: cached in Redis (group_id → member list) with 5-min TTL; invalidated on member add/remove.
- **Connection lookup**: Redis `device_id → server_id` map; updated on connect/disconnect.
- **Recent messages**: per-user LRU cache of last 50 messages in Redis (for quick scroll-back without DB hit).
- **No caching of ciphertext**: messages are end-to-end encrypted, so caching at the server is safe (no plaintext exposed), but adds no value beyond DB cache.

### Failure Modes
| Failure | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Connection server crash | All sockets on that node drop | Load balancer health check; clients auto-reconnect with exponential backoff; offline queue catches missed messages |
| Cassandra node down | Some mailboxes temporarily unavailable | RF=3, quorum reads/writes, automatic repair |
| Redis (presence) down | Presence updates lag, "online" status stale | Redis Cluster with sentinel failover; fall back to "last_seen_at" from Postgres |
| Kafka broker down | Push notification + analytics lag, real-time messaging unaffected | 3 brokers RF=3, min ISR=2 |
| Region outage | 50% of users disconnected | Multi-region active-active; DNS failover to healthy region; clients reconnect |
| Key server (KMS) down | New conversations can't establish E2EE | Pre-key bundles pre-cached in Redis for 24 h; clients fetch in advance |
| Group with 1 024 members all online | Fanout storm on every message | Batch via Kafka topic per group; rate-limit sender to 10 msgs/min in big groups |
| Client clock skew | Sequence number collisions | Snowflake uses server-side timestamp, not client; clients trust server timestamps |
